facts.statement: Tynskya is an extinct genus of bird belonging to the family Messelasturidae.
facts.quote: Tynskya is an extinct genus of messelasturid bird.

facts.statement: The genus Tynskya was first described in 2000 by the paleontologist Gerald Mayr.
facts.quote: Tynskya was first described in 2000 by Gerald Mayr.

facts.statement: The type species Tynskya eocaena was named based on an incomplete articulated skeleton found in the Tynsky quarry within the Green River Formation of Wyoming, USA.
facts.quote: The holotype BSP 1997 I 6 is an incomplete articulated skeleton, dug up in Tynsky quarry in the Green River formation, Wyoming, USA.

facts.statement: The genus name Tynskya honors the Tynsky quarry where the type specimen was discovered, while the species epithet eocaena refers to the time period in which the animal lived.
facts.quote: The genus name was named after the quarry it was found in and the epithet was named after the time period the species lived in.

facts.statement: A second species, Tynskya waltonensis, was described in 2021 based on a partial skeleton.
facts.quote: Then in 2021 another species T. waltonensis described based on a partial skeleton.

facts.statement: The holotype for Tynskya waltonensis was originally discovered in 1986 by Paul Bergdhal in Walton-on-the-Naze, England, within the London Clay formation.
facts.quote: The holotype SMF Av 652 is a specimen originally found in Walton-on-the-Naze, London Clay in 1986 by Paul Bergdhal which was originally categorized as BC 8611.

facts.statement: Two additional species, Tynskya crassitarsus and Tynskya brevitarsus, were described in 2023 based on partial skeletons.
facts.quote: Then in 2023, two other species would be described T. crassitarsus and T. brevitarsus, both being described by partial skeletons.

facts.statement: The species name T. crassitarsus refers to its thick tarsometatarsus, while T. brevitarsus refers to its short tarsometatarsus.
facts.quote: The epithet for T. crassitarsus is derived from the Latin word crassus which means "thick" and refers to its thick tarsometatarsus and the epithet for T. brevitarsus is derived from the Latin word brevis which means "short", referring to the species short tarsometatarsus.

facts.statement: Isolated bones of Tynskya have been found in the London Clay formation.
facts.quote: Another referred specimen (WN 96939) was found in London Clay based on isolated bones.

facts.statement: Fossils of the type species Tynskya eocaena are known from the Green River Formation in North America.
facts.quote: T. eocaena, the type species, is known from fossils found in the North American Green River Formation.

facts.statement: The species Tynskya waltonensis, Tynskya brevitarsus, and Tynskya crassitarsus are found in the Walton Member of the London Clay Formation in England.
facts.quote: The Walton Member of the London Clay Formation of England contains the species T. waltonensis, along with the more recently described T. brevitarsus and T. crassitarsus.

facts.statement: Tynskya lived during the Ypresian stage, approximately 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Ypresian (56 to 48.07 million years ago)

facts.statement: Tynskya belongs to the parent group Messelasturidae.
The family classification for Tynskya is Messelasturidae.

rejected.statement: Tynskya is classified within the class Aves (birds).
